title: Feinberg v. Pfeiffer Co.
lead: A company promises a veteran employee a pension she may claim whenever she retires. Years after she gives up her job in reliance on it, new management cuts the payment and disputes any legal obligation.

actors.name: Anna Sacks Feinberg
actors.role: Longtime bookkeeper, office manager and assistant treasurer; pension claimant.

actors.name: Pfeiffer Company
actors.role: Pharmaceutical manufacturer that promised the pension.

actors.name: Max Lippman
actors.role: President when the board approved the resolution.

actors.name: Sidney Harris and Sol Flammer
actors.role: Directors who communicated it; Harris later became president and reduced payment.

proceedings: The St. Louis circuit court tried the case without a jury and awarded $5,100 accrued installments plus interest.
The Missouri Court of Appeals affirmed on March 17, 1959; rehearing or transfer was denied April 13.
limits: This narrative follows the canonical historical brief without a new opinion audit. Liability rested on the healthy 1949 retirement, not later cancer. The judgment covered accrued installments and interest. The later Second Restatement’s flexible-remedy language was not the First Restatement formulation applied in 1959.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: The board promises retirement income after thirty-seven years of service
sections.cue: What did Feinberg promise in exchange, if anything?
paragraphs: Anna Sacks Feinberg joined the pharmaceutical manufacturer Pfeiffer in 1910 at seventeen. By 1947 she was bookkeeper, office manager and assistant treasurer. She owned seventy of 6,503 shares: twenty received as gifts, twenty purchased and thirty from a stock split or dividend. She received stock dividends and employee bonuses from 1937 through 1949 ranging from $300 to $2,000.

On December 27, 1947, President Max Lippman presided over a board meeting whose five attending directors owned 5,007 shares. Recognizing Feinberg’s long, faithful and skilled service, they raised her monthly salary from $350 to $400 and adopted a retirement privilege intended as a firm corporate obligation and future security. She could retire whenever she chose and receive $200 monthly for life. The resolution expressed hope that she would remain for years, without requiring it.

At Lippman’s request, directors Sidney Harris and Sol Flammer told her that day. She had no advance notice and was surprised. She understood retirement was immediately available. Employment remained at will: she promised no further service, and the company could discharge her. She later testified that she would have continued working even without the resolution.

sections.title: Feinberg retires in reliance on the promised support
sections.cue: How did the company’s later change of management produce a dispute?
paragraphs: Feinberg continued until June 30, 1949, then retired at fifty-seven while healthy and able to work. She and her husband calculated that his earnings and the pension would support them. She testified she would have stayed employed without the pension. While payments continued, she sought no other work.

Pfeiffer paid $200 on the first of each month. Lippman died November 18, 1949. His widow became president and continued the checks, though she personally regarded them as gifts. Harris became president in October 1953. New accountants Ernst & Ernst repeatedly questioned the payments, and in spring 1956 Harris consulted attorney Ralph Kalish. Harris testified that the advisers said payment was not legally required.
On April 1, 1956, the company sent only $100. Feinberg declined that reduction and sued. Her action sought enforcement of the $200 lifetime promise rather than acceptance of a discretionary gift.

sections.title: The trial court credits reliance and awards accrued installments
sections.cue: Why did her illness at trial not supply the foundation of the claim?
paragraphs: The parties waived a jury in the Circuit Court of the City of St. Louis. The court found for Feinberg and awarded $5,100 in installments accrued through trial plus interest. Pfeiffer appealed evidentiary rulings, the reliance finding and enforceability.

At trial Feinberg was sixty-five and one-half and unable to work following cancer removal and an operation on November 25, 1957. Pfeiffer argued that the judge improperly relied on that condition. Missouri’s review statute required the appellate court to review law and evidence and enter the judgment that should have been entered. It considered admissible evidence and located the inducing event in her healthy 1949 retirement, years before illness.

The credited testimony showed that Feinberg could have continued, used the pension to plan household income and would have stayed without it. The eighteen-month interval before retirement did not negate actual inducement.

sources.pinpoint: Procedural History; Material Facts; actual-inducement reasoning; 322 S.W.2d 163–166, 169

sections.title: Past service and continued employment do not supply a bargain
sections.cue: Why did consideration fail while promissory estoppel succeed?
paragraphs: The completed thirty-seven years explained corporate gratitude but could not have been exchanged for a later promise. Nor did the additional eighteen months create consideration. Feinberg could retire immediately, the board merely hoped she would stay, and she undertook no reciprocal service obligation.

The court instead applied First Restatement § 90: a promise becomes binding when the promisor should reasonably expect definite and substantial action or forbearance, it actually induces that response, and enforcement is necessary to avoid injustice. Retirement was exactly what this retirement privilege contemplated. The company could foresee surrender of salary in reliance on lifetime income.

Feinberg relinquished a lucrative, long-held position at fifty-seven and organized her life around payment. Pfeiffer continued nearly seven years before cutting it, when she was over sixty-three and comparable work was realistically difficult to obtain. Retirement, lost opportunities and elapsed employable years made the reliance substantial. Later illness reinforced the practical consequences but did not control the promise’s binding effect.

The court found Ricketts’s promise-induced departure from employment closely analogous. Missouri decisions had variously called induced conduct consideration, estoppel, or an implied return promise; § 90 and promissory estoppel best explained this enforcement without a bargain.

sections.title: The appellate court preserves the pension judgment
paragraphs: Commissioner Doerner recommended affirmance, and the court adopted his opinion per curiam on March 17, 1959. Presiding Judge Wolfe and Judges Anderson and Ruddy concurred; no separate writing appeared. Rehearing or transfer to the Missouri Supreme Court was denied April 13.

The affirmed judgment was $5,100 in accrued pension installments plus interest. Enforcing the lifetime undertaking answered the reliance caused by surrender of employment, but the court did not adjudicate every possible remedy under later doctrine. The subsequently reproduced Second Restatement permits relief limited as justice requires; that wording was not part of the First Restatement rule this court quoted and applied.
